about: Combining must accept its own output.
`compose` rejects a statement that was already impossible on its own — a
floor above its own ceiling is a typo, and calling it a collision hides
it. That check is right at the front door and wrong everywhere else: it
made `compose` REFUSE ITS OWN RESULT the moment two statements collided.
An operation that cannot take its own output back is not closed, and
without closure there is exactly one legal way to evaluate: a single pass
over the original statements. No folding in a tree, no combining partial
results from shards, no merging replicas that were partitioned. The whole
reason this arithmetic is worth having is that order does not matter, and
an operation you can only apply left to right does not deliver that.
So `fuse` carries the law and `compose` is `fuse` plus an entry check.
The five properties below are the merge law of a conflict-free replicated
type, which is why a crossed result must survive rather than be resolved
away: both sides were load-bearing, and a winner is not an answer.

coverage.criterion: each property once, plus both directions of the compose/fuse split on the same input
coverage.why: the properties are checked exhaustively over a small scale in the runner; these cases pin the intent and the split, not the whole space

cases.name: crossed result is returned, not refused
and that result may be combined again
a malformed statement from a caller is still an error
nothing to combine is the neutral element
the same statement twice changes nothing
